Orbit. The curved path traced by an object as it moves under the influence of gravity from a massive central body. Described mathematically by Newton's laws and gravitational force, orbits are conic sections—ellipses, circles, parabolas, and hyperbolas—depending on the object's energy and angular momentum. Planets orbit stars, moons orbit planets, and artificial satellites orbit Earth, all following the same gravitational principles. Understanding orbits is essential to celestial mechanics, space exploration, and predicting the motion of celestial bodies.

Elliptical orbits dominate. Planets, moons, and satellites follow ellipses with the primary, whether star or planet, at one focus. A circular orbit is a special case with both foci coincident. Orbital period follows Kepler's third law: the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. Mars, farther from the Sun than Earth, takes longer to orbit, proportional to the cube root of its distance.

Aphelion, or apogee for Earth satellites, is the farthest point in an orbit. Perihelion, or perigee, is the nearest. The difference defines orbital eccentricity, ranging from zero for a circle to one for a parabola at escape velocity. Escape velocity from Earth is approximately 11.2 kilometers per second. Objects below this speed remain bound and orbit. Above it, they follow hyperbolic paths and escape the gravitational well.

Retrograde orbits are unusual, moving counter to the primary's rotation. They arise from gravitational capture of asteroids or from deliberate orbital maneuvers in spacecraft for interplanetary transfers. Orbital velocity decreases with altitude. Low Earth orbit satellites move at approximately seven-point-eight kilometers per second. The Moon, 384,000 kilometers away, moves only about one kilometer per second around Earth.

Orbital decay occurs when atmospheric drag or other perturbations remove energy. Low-orbit satellites gradually spiral downward until atmospheric reentry. Orbital resonance occurs when orbital periods share integer ratios, such as Neptune's moon Triton orbiting in a one-to-one resonance with Neptune's rotation, causing tidal heating. This drives orbital dynamics and stability in multi-body systems.
